narrative.note: This report catches Riley right at the start of a lot of new skills, which is completely normal for four, and there's plenty of exciting growth just ahead.

subjects.math: Right now, counting one object at a time and saying how many there are altogether is where Riley's math is heading next.
subjects.literacy: Riley is starting to notice that print carries meaning, like wondering what a sign or cereal box says, which is the next spark for literacy.
subjects.phonics: Clapping out the beats in a word, like ba-na-na, is the next phonics skill coming into view for Riley.
subjects.writing: Switching from a fist grip to holding a crayon with their fingers is the next step in Riley's writing.
subjects.language: Telling you about something that happened earlier today, holding that whole story in mind, is the next reach for Riley's language.
subjects.science: Sorting things into groups, big versus small, animals versus plants, is next up for Riley's science.
subjects.social_studies: Understanding how family members connect, like how grandma is mommy's mom, is the next piece of social studies for Riley.
subjects.art: Naming the main colors while drawing or painting is next for Riley's art.
subjects.music: Clapping or tapping along to a steady beat is the next music skill for Riley to build.
subjects.gross_motor: Riley's next move in gross motor is galloping, with one foot leading the other.
subjects.fine_motor: Threading laces or stringing large beads is the next fine motor task on the horizon for Riley.
subjects.social_emotional: Riley is working toward playing WITH other kids, taking turns and sharing with reminders.
subjects.self_care: Riley's next self-care milestone is using the toilet during the day, with only the occasional miss.
subjects.executive_function: Riley's next stretch in executive function is waiting a short turn without falling apart, even with support.
subjects.computer_science: Coding and computers are wide open for Riley, ready whenever it fits into your days.
subjects.spanish: A second language is wide open too, ready whenever you want to bring it into Riley's days.

drawers.math: That one-by-one counting bridges naming numbers and truly understanding what they mean. Try counting trucks, stairs, or crackers together, touching each one as you count, and beat yesterday's number by one.
drawers.literacy: Curiosity about words usually comes before recognizing letters, so noticing print now sets up decoding later. A daily letter hunt keeps it playful: pick one letter and spot it everywhere you go today.
drawers.phonics: Hearing syllables is an early ear-training step before sounds and letters connect. Sound I-spy works well too: 'I spy something that starts with mmm' turns car rides into practice.
drawers.writing: That grip shift takes hand strength that builds through play, not more writing time. Try the rainbow name: write Riley's name big, then let them trace it in two more colors before decorating it.
drawers.language: That kind of storytelling asks a child to hold time in their head, which is a real leap at four. After anything fun, hand Riley the story: 'tell me what happened at the park,' and let them narrate while you add the oohs.
drawers.science: Sorting is early classification, the same thinking scientists use to organize the world. Sink or float works well too: gather five small things, guess before each one goes in, and let the guessing be the science.
drawers.social_studies: That kind of relationship mapping is abstract for a four-year-old, so it's a fair next stretch. Drawing a map of your home together, with a star for everyone's bed, gives Riley a first map and a first legend with zero prep.
drawers.art: Color words often come later than color recognition itself, so this is more about vocabulary than seeing. Play one song and have Riley draw how it feels: fast scribbles for fast parts, soft colors for quiet ones.
drawers.music: Keeping a steady beat is a physical skill that takes practice, not just listening. Copy my clap turns it into a game: clap a short pattern, let Riley echo it, then swap who leads.
drawers.gross_motor: Galloping asks for a new kind of balance and rhythm past a simple run. Animal races down the hallway, bear crawl, crab walk, frog jump, make that practice feel like a game.
drawers.fine_motor: That threading motion builds the same hand control used later for buttons and zippers. Snipping strips of paper into a jar works well in the meantime, five minutes with child-safe scissors.
drawers.social_emotional: Cooperative play like that is still new at four, and reminders are expected, not a sign of trouble. When big feelings come up, naming the feeling first, then offering two choices, is often half the calming.
drawers.self_care: This one is as much about readiness as timing, and it can click quickly once it starts. The button board turns practice into a game: button an old shirt around a cushion and race the timer instead of each other.
drawers.executive_function: Waiting is one of the hardest skills at this age because it asks a child to manage a feeling and a body at once. Freeze dance makes it playful: music on to dance big, music off to freeze.
drawers.computer_science: This one is about exposure, not a timeline, so there's no rush here. Robot parent is a fun way in: Riley programs you across the room with exact steps, wrong steps included, and debugging starts as giggles.
drawers.spanish: Exposure at this age is about the words that show up in daily life, not fluency. Picking one useful phrase and using it all week at natural moments helps it actually stick.
